prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in it, which opened the field of moire quantum materials.

statement.case_for: After the full first round I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, and for the same scientific reason. A single geometric parameter, the twist angle, tunes a band structure into a flat-band regime in which correlated insulators and gate-tunable superconductivity appear, and this was predicted (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) before it was found (Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators, 2018). The discovery credited is the existence of those phases at the magic angle, not the pairing mechanism, and that core is reproduced by many independent groups and across several moire platforms. The chair's second question has a straightforward answer for me: the open mechanism bears on timing and on what the citation may claim, not on whether a discovery was made. Earlier prizes honoured established phenomena before their microscopic explanation was settled. I therefore support a citation confined to the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated and superconducting states, with no mechanism and no claim about moire physics at large in the credited wording.
statement.case_against: The reservations that remain are real. About eight years have passed, twist-angle disorder makes sample quality uneven, and the pairing mechanism is open, so a cautious committee can reasonably call this the youngest case on the shortlist. The attribution is also not airtight: Eva Andrei's scanning-probe work on flat bands and van Hove singularities in twisted bilayers is a documented experimental contribution that a three-name cap forces out. If the committee decides that maturity must outweigh originality, B013 is the better-confirmed fallback, though its credit is compound (Hasan, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang) and it sits near the 2016 topology prize. B006 is mature and cleanly attributed but, to my judgement, a refinement of the metrology honoured in 2005 and 2012.

responses.point: Johansson moved to the Bistritzer, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero trio but keeps Andrei's claim open, and worries that leaving her out may look arbitrary in hindsight.
responses.response: I am glad we now agree on names, and I share the discomfort. I still hold that the three-name set should be the two originators of the continuum model plus the experiment that found the phases. Andrei's early STM work showed renormalised Dirac velocities and van Hove singularities at small angle, which is evidence consistent with flat bands but neither the prediction of the magic angle nor the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states. A citation worded around those two items makes the credit logic explicit and defensible. I would revisit this only if someone shows that her data was decisive for the correlated-phase discovery itself, which I do not believe it was.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from B033 to B013 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and stresses that the pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder make B025 premature.
responses.response: Your move to Mele was right, and the Kane-Mele paper is the conceptual core of B013, so I treat that configuration as the best alternative. Where we differ is on the standard of maturity. Nearly two decades of confirmation is better than eight years, I accept that, but the standard should be the stability of the discovered phenomenon, not the completeness of its explanation. Correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle have been reproduced repeatedly, including in other moire systems. I also note that you accept the 2016 overlap concern for topology as an open question, so the novelty argument does not run only in my direction. I would not call B013 inferior; I would call it the safer prize and B025 the more original one.

responses.point: Lindroth asks for consistent treatment of recent prizes in nearby fields and cautions that a clock prize should not hinge on the undecided redefinition of the second; she also reminds us that familiarity with one's own field is not consensus.
responses.response: I accept the call for a field-neutral rule and I will state mine: a recent prize in a neighbouring field lowers novelty only where the new citation would cover the same discovery. By that rule the 2016 topology prize bears weakly on B013, the 2025 circuits prize bears on B009 but not on B025, and the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes bear moderately on B006 because the lattice clock builds on comb and trapped-ion control. I also take your point about vantage seriously, and I disclose that mine is adjacent to B025. Your argument that B006 is timely and cannot be called premature is the strongest case against my ordering, and I would not oppose it if the committee prefers maturity to novelty.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock changed the statistical and systematic regime of frequency metrology, that it is not a gradual refinement, and that its two-name attribution is clean.
responses.response: I accept that magic-wavelength trapping with thousands of atoms is a genuine change of regime and that the attribution is the cleanest on the list, which is why B006 stays among my alternatives. My disagreement is about what kind of prize it is. It improves a measurement on atomic transitions we understand, while twisted bilayer graphene opened a regime of correlated electrons that nobody had seen. You and Lindroth also note that the redefinition of the second is undecided and that the Paris and PTB groups sit outside the two names. Neither is disqualifying, but together they leave me preferring B025 unless the committee deliberately wants a metrology prize.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B013 as the least contested on names and the best confirmed, but concedes that Hasan's three-dimensional work and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction are outside the credited trio.
responses.response: I agree that the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio is the strongest topological configuration and that it has the broadest name agreement. You list a compound credit yourself: Hasan's three-dimensional discovery and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction that made the HgTe experiment possible fall outside it, so a three-person prize cannot honestly cover everything the word topological insulator now stands for. B025 has its own contested third seat, but the discovery credited there has fewer separable parts. That is why I rank B025 first, while expecting B013 to be a strong future prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept Bistritzer or Andrei as the third laureate; I rely on recall of the historical record rather than verification, and I did not hear evidence in round 1 that settles it.
Whether the unresolved superconducting mechanism and twist-angle disorder justify waiting a few years, which I weigh as a timing issue not a question of whether a discovery was made.
How much the 2016 topological-phases prize should weigh on B013, and the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes on B006, under a common rule.
I still form no view on the astrophysical candidates (B040, B008) and do not carry either into my final position.
statement.conflict_note: My work on electronic structure of two-dimensional materials and magnetism is adjacent to twisted bilayer graphene, which could bias me toward B025, and I flag that for colleagues. I have no documented personal or institutional tie to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer or Andrei in my profile. I chaired the 2025 committee that awarded the superconducting-circuits prize, which bears on B009, not on my configuration, and I do not regard it as a recusal matter. My round-1 disclosure is otherwise unchanged.
